DOCUMENT:
Market Analysis: Launching a Digital Subscription for the Calderbrook Courier
Commercial Strategy, Calderbrook Media, April 2026

1. Purpose
The Calderbrook Courier's website is free to read and funded by display advertising, which has declined by about 12% a year for three years. This paper assesses the market for a metered digital subscription, in which readers can view five articles a month free before being asked to subscribe, and recommends a price and launch plan.

2. Our audience
The website had an average of 420,000 monthly unique users (MUU) in 2025, of whom around 60% live in the Courier's circulation area. The printed Courier has 11,200 subscribers paying £18.50 a month for six-day home delivery, plus around 6,000 daily news-stand sales. Print subscribers are older on average than web readers, and most also use the website.

In our March 2026 survey of print subscribers (1,850 responses), 30% said they would cancel their print subscription and take a digital-only subscription instead if one were offered at under £6 a month.

3. Evidence from comparable titles
We obtained data, under confidentiality agreements, from four regional titles that launched metered subscriptions between 2022 and 2024.

Table 1. Comparable regional titles, second year after launch
Title | Monthly unique users | Digital subscribers | Subscribers as % of MUU | Monthly price
Title A | 360,000 | 6,800 | 1.9% | £5.99
Title B | 280,000 | 3,100 | 1.1% | £4.99
Title C | 390,000 | 9,400 | 2.4% | £7.99
Title D | 300,000 | 4,200 | 1.4% | £3.99

All four titles reported that subscriber numbers stabilised by the end of the second year, and that churn settled at between 3% and 5% a month after promotional periods ended.

4. Price
Conversion rates across the comparable titles are highest for the titles charging the lowest prices, which suggests that our audience will respond best to a low price point. We therefore propose a price of £4.99 a month, with an introductory offer of £1 for the first three months.

5. Projection
The average conversion rate of the four comparable titles is 2.0% of MUU. Applied to our 420,000 MUU, that gives about 8,400 subscribers by the end of year two. At £4.99 a month, 8,400 subscribers would generate around £503,000 a year in subscription revenue.

Table 2. Year-two projection
Item | Annual amount
Subscription revenue | £503,000
Subscription platform and payment fees | £85,000
Marketing | £60,000
Net contribution | £358,000

We expect a modest reduction in display advertising revenue as page views from non-subscribers fall when they reach the meter; the comparable titles reported falls of 5% to 8% in page views. Our display revenue was £1.1 million in 2025, so a fall of this size would cost between £55,000 and £88,000 a year, which is well covered by the projected net contribution.

6. Launch plan
- Platform selection and integration: May to July 2026.
- Soft launch with a ten-article meter: September 2026.
- Full launch with a five-article meter: November 2026.
- Review of price and meter after six months.

7. Conclusion
The evidence from comparable titles shows a viable market for a Courier digital subscription. At £4.99 a month, a price that the comparable titles' experience suggests will maximise take-up, we project around 8,400 subscribers and a net contribution of £358,000 a year, more than offsetting the expected effect on display advertising. We recommend approval to proceed with the launch plan.

KEY (three known flaws):
1. [arithmetic] at: "The average conversion rate of the four comparable titles is 2.0% of MUU." -- (1.9 + 1.1 + 2.4 + 1.4) / 4 = 1.7%, not 2.0%. At 1.7% the projection is about 7,140 subscribers, not 8,400, and revenue about £428,000.
2. [misread_evidence] at: "Conversion rates across the comparable titles are highest for the titles charging the lowest prices" -- Table 1 shows the opposite pattern: the highest-priced title (C, £7.99) has the highest conversion (2.4%) and the lowest-priced (D, £3.99) has 1.4%. The pricing rationale rests on misreading the table.
3. [missing_consideration] at: "At £4.99 a month, 8,400 subscribers would generate around £503,000 a year in subscription revenue." -- The projection treats all subscription revenue as incremental, but the document's own survey says 30% of the 11,200 print subscribers (about 3,360) would cancel £18.50 print subscriptions for a digital one under £6. Switching would cost about £13.51 a month each (roughly £545,000 a year), which is never addressed although it could wipe out the net contribution.

REVIEW:
# Review: Calderbrook Courier digital subscription analysis

The case is weaker than the author's description suggests. Two of its central claims are contradicted by the document's own Table 1, and a large cost is left out of the projection.

## Major problems

**1. The price argument is backwards.**
Section 4 says conversion is highest for the lowest-priced titles. Table 1 shows the opposite:

| Title | Price | Conversion |
|---|---|---|
| C | £7.99 | 2.4% |
| A | £5.99 | 1.9% |
| D | £3.99 | 1.4% |
| B | £4.99 | 1.1% |

Conversion generally rises with price, and the £4.99 title has the lowest conversion of all four. With n=4 and obvious confounders (brand strength, content, meter design, promotions), the table cannot show that a low price maximises take-up. It certainly does not support that claim. The recommendation of £4.99 and the conclusion's "maximise take-up" line have no evidential basis. The paper may also be underpricing: the data hint that a higher price could yield more subscribers and more revenue per subscriber.

**2. The average conversion rate is miscalculated.**
The four rates (1.9, 1.1, 2.4, 1.4) average 1.7%, not 2.0%. The weighted figure is 23,500 / 1,330,000 ≈ 1.77%. At 1.7%, the Courier would reach about 7,100 subscribers, not 8,400. The closest price comparator, Title B at £4.99, converted at 1.1%, which would mean about 4,600 subscribers and roughly £277k of revenue. That is nearly half the headline figure.

**3. Print cannibalisation is not costed.**
Section 2 reports that 30% of surveyed print subscribers would switch to digital-only below £6, but the survey never appears in the projection. If 30% of 11,200 print subscribers switched (about 3,360), the lost print revenue would be about £746k a year (£18.50 × 12 × 3,360). That is larger than the entire projected subscription revenue and would turn the "net contribution" negative. Even a fraction of that switching would erode much of the gain. The claim that the display loss is "explicitly costed" is true, but the larger cost is ignored. Because stated intent in a self-selected survey overstates real behaviour, the paper should model a range of switching rates rather than leave the issue out. The 8,400 subscribers may also include these switchers, so some of the digital revenue would not be new revenue.

**4. Year-two revenue is overstated.**
- £503k assumes 8,400 subscribers each paying £4.99 for all 12 months. 8,400 is the end-of-year-two figure, so the average over the year would be lower.
- It ignores the £1 introductory offer for three months.
- It ignores churn of 3–5% a month, which means roughly a third to a half of the base must be replaced every year. A flat £60k marketing budget may not sustain that, and the paper does not model it.

## Other concerns

- **Applicability of the comparables.** The paper does not say whether the comparables' MUU counts are comparable (for example, local versus total audience). Only about 60% of Courier users (about 252k) live in the circulation area. It also does not say whether their meters, launch phasing or promotions matched the Courier's. A softer ten-article meter at first launch would also lower conversion.
- **Sample and verifiability.** Four titles under confidentiality cannot be checked, and the paper gives no range or sensitivity analysis.
- **Display loss assumption.** The 5–8% page-view fall is assumed to translate one-for-one into display revenue. The paper does not test this, and the existing 12% annual decline is not separated from the meter effect.
- **Overlap with print.** Most print subscribers already use the website, so they sit inside the 420k base. This adds to the cannibalisation risk and may inflate the addressable audience.
- **Framing.** "Comfortably covers" and "a well-evidenced case" overstate what the analysis supports.

## Recommendation

Do not approve on this basis. The paper should:

1. Recompute the average conversion (about 1.7%).
2. Remove or correct the claim that low prices drive conversion, and test other price points such as £5.99 and £7.99.
3. Add a print-cannibalisation scenario using the survey.
4. Build a month-by-month model with promotional pricing, churn and ramp-up.
5. Present low, base and high cases rather than a single point estimate.
